title: Reading & Decoding METARs and SPECIs

required_knowledge_points.title: METAR Structure — The Eight Element Decode
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE will hand the applicant a raw METAR and ask for a full decode. Every element has a specific AGL/MSL distinction, a wind direction true-versus-magnetic nuance, and a sky condition shorthand that applicants routinely confuse.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: METAR (Meteorological Aerodrome Report) is issued hourly. Eight primary elements in order: (1) Type — METAR (routine) or SPECI (special, off-cycle). (2) Station ID — 4-letter ICAO identifier. (3) Date/Time — 6-digit group: DDHHMMZ in UTC (Zulu). (4) Wind — direction in TRUE degrees, speed in knots, gusts if applicable. Calm: 00000KT. Variable <3 kts: VRB01KT. (5) Visibility — statute miles and fractions. (6) Weather — present weather codes. (7) Sky Condition — FEW/SCT/BKN/OVC in hundreds of feet AGL. (8) Temp/Dewpoint in Celsius. (9) Altimeter — preceded by A in inHg.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### METAR Elements — In Order

| # | Element | Format | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Type** | METAR (routine) or SPECI (special) | `METAR` |
| 2 | **Station ID** | 4-letter ICAO identifier | `KATL` |
| 3 | **Date/Time** | DDHHMMZ in **UTC (Zulu)** | `121855Z` |
| 4 | **Wind** | Direction in **TRUE** degrees / speed KT / gusts | `27015G25KT` |
| 5 | **Visibility** | Statute miles and fractions | `10SM` or `1 1/2SM` |
| 6 | **Weather** | Present weather codes (RA, SN, FG, TS, BR, HZ) | `-RA` |
| 7 | **Sky Condition** | FEW/SCT/BKN/OVC + height in **hundreds of feet AGL** | `BKN045` |
| 8 | **Temp/Dewpoint** | Celsius; M prefix = minus | `22/14` or `M04/M08` |
| 9 | **Altimeter** | Preceded by `A`, in inHg | `A2992` |

### Special Wind Codes
- **00000KT** = Calm
- **VRB01KT** = Variable direction, less than 3 knots

required_knowledge_points.title: METAR Wind Direction — TRUE Not Magnetic
required_knowledge_points.why: The most reliable METAR oral exam trap: 'The METAR reports winds from 270 — what heading do you set on your DI to fly directly into the wind?' A student who understands the True/Magnetic distinction demonstrates deeper knowledge the DPE rewards.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Wind direction in METAR text reports is given relative to TRUE NORTH, not magnetic north. A pilot must apply magnetic variation to convert the METAR's true wind direction to a magnetic heading for navigation. Example: METAR winds 270°T, magnetic variation 10°E → Magnetic wind = 270° - 10° = 260°M. Important contrast: ASOS/AWOS/ATIS voice broadcasts report winds in MAGNETIC degrees. Text METARs and TAFs use TRUE degrees. Winds Aloft forecasts (FB) also use True North.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Wind Direction Convention
- **METAR text reports:** Wind direction in **TRUE** degrees
- **ATIS / ASOS / AWOS voice broadcasts:** Wind direction in **MAGNETIC** degrees (to align with runway designations)
- **Winds Aloft Forecasts (FB):** Wind direction in **TRUE** degrees

### Converting for Navigation — Worked Example
| | Value |
|---|---|
| METAR wind direction | 270°**T** |
| Magnetic variation | 10°E |
| Rule: East is Least (subtract) | 270° − 10° = **260°M** |
| Best runway for landing | The one closest to **260° Magnetic** |

> The ATIS at the same airport would report winds from **260°** (magnetic) — confirming the conversion

required_knowledge_points.title: Sky Condition Decode — AGL Heights and Ceiling Determination
required_knowledge_points.why: An applicant who reads 'BKN045' and says 'broken clouds at 4,500 feet MSL' has failed. All METAR sky condition heights are AGL. The DPE is listening for AGL. Additionally, the first BKN or OVC layer defines the ceiling.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: METAR sky condition codes: FEW = 1/8 to 2/8 coverage. SCT = 3/8 to 4/8. BKN = 5/8 to 7/8 (broken — this is a ceiling). OVC = 8/8 (overcast — this is a ceiling). All heights are in HUNDREDS of feet ABOVE GROUND LEVEL. BKN045 = broken ceiling at 4,500 feet AGL. The CEILING is the lowest broken or overcast layer. Flight categories: VFR = ceiling above 3,000 AGL AND visibility >5SM. MVFR = ceiling 1,000–3,000 AGL OR visibility 3–5SM. IFR = ceiling 500–999 AGL OR visibility 1–3SM. LIFR = ceiling <500 AGL OR visibility <1SM.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Sky Condition Codes — Coverage and Ceiling Status
| Code | Coverage | Is It a Ceiling? |
|---|---|---|
| **FEW** | 1/8 – 2/8 | **No** |
| **SCT** | 3/8 – 4/8 | **No** |
| **BKN** | 5/8 – 7/8 | **Yes** |
| **OVC** | 8/8 (overcast) | **Yes** |
| **VV** | Vertical visibility into obscuration | **Yes** |

- All heights = **hundreds of feet AGL** (not MSL) — BKN045 = ceiling at **4,500 feet AGL**
- **Ceiling** = the lowest BKN, OVC, or VV layer

### Flight Category Thresholds
| Category | Ceiling | OR Visibility |
|---|---|---|
| **LIFR** | < 500 AGL | < 1 SM |
| **IFR** | 500–999 AGL | 1–3 SM |
| **MVFR** | 1,000–3,000 AGL | 3–5 SM |
| **VFR** | > 3,000 AGL | > 5 SM |

required_knowledge_points.title: SPECI — When and Why a Special Report Is Issued
required_knowledge_points.why: Most applicants know what a METAR is but cannot explain SPECI. The DPE specifically rewards students who understand the trigger conditions for a special report because it demonstrates awareness of rapidly deteriorating weather.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: A SPECI (Special METAR) is issued off-cycle whenever defined threshold changes in weather conditions occur and the next routine METAR is more than 15 minutes away. SPECI issuance triggers include: tornado/funnel cloud/waterspout; thunderstorms begin or end; precipitation type changes; hail at station; visibility falls through VFR/MVFR/IFR/LIFR thresholds (3SM, 2SM, 1SM, 1/2SM); ceiling falls through 3,000, 1,500, 1,000, or 500 feet AGL; wind shift of 45° or more at 10 knots or greater.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### SPECI — Special METAR
- Issued **off-cycle** when conditions change rapidly and the next METAR is more than **15 minutes away**
- Issued in **addition to** routine hourly METARs — not instead of them

### Issuance Triggers
- **Tornado, funnel cloud, or waterspout** observed or ended
- **Thunderstorm** begins or ends
- **Precipitation type changes** (e.g., rain to freezing rain)
- **Hail** reported at the station
- **Visibility** falls or rises through: 3SM, 2SM, 1SM, or 1/2SM
- **Ceiling** falls or rises through: 3,000, 1,500, 1,000, or 500 ft AGL
- **Wind shift** of ≥ **45°** when sustained wind ≥ **10 knots**

> Pilots who obtain only a routine METAR may miss a SPECI that captures a rapid IFR condition change in the 45 minutes before arrival — a known factor in several VFR-into-IMC accidents

lesson_overview:
## METARs — Decoding the Language of Airport Weather

A METAR is the single most important weather document a VFR pilot will read before a flight. It tells you what the weather is *right now* at a specific reporting station. It's also one of the richest sources of checkride oral questions, because it looks completely alien until you learn the code — and then it's blindingly logical. Let's make it logical.

**The anatomy of a METAR.** Here's a complete example to anchor everything:

`METAR KATL 121855Z 27015G25KT 10SM BKN050 OVC080 22/14 A2998 RMK AO2 SLP152`

Every field means something specific. In order:

- **KATL** — ICAO station identifier (Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson). U.S. airports use K-prefix + 3-letter FAA code.
- **121855Z** — Day 12, time 1855 UTC (Zulu). Every METAR time is Zulu. Full stop.
- **27015G25KT** — Wind from 270° true at 15 knots, gusting to 25 knots. True degrees (not magnetic — different from compass work).
- **10SM** — Flight visibility 10 statute miles. Anything below 3 SM triggers an MVFR condition.
- **BKN050 OVC080** — Broken ceiling at 5,000 feet AGL (multiply hundreds by 100), overcast at 8,000 feet AGL. Ceiling is the lowest BKN or OVC layer.
- **22/14** — Temperature 22°C / Dewpoint 14°C. Spread of 8°C: fog probability is low. When spread closes to 2-3°C, fog or low cloud is imminent.
- **A2998** — Altimeter setting: 29.98 in Hg.
- **RMK AO2** — Remarks, Automated station with precipitation sensor.
- **SLP152** — Sea Level Pressure 1015.2 hPa (for meteorological analysis).

**Sky condition codes.** The four you need cold: **FEW** (1-2 oktas coverage — not a ceiling), **SCT** (Scattered, 3-4 oktas — not a ceiling), **BKN** (Broken, 5-7 oktas — this IS a ceiling), **OVC** (Overcast, 8 oktas — ceiling). Only BKN, OVC, and VV (Vertical Visibility) define an official ceiling for VFR/IFR categorization purposes. **VV** appears when the sky is obscured (fog, smoke, precipitation) and a human observer can't see discrete cloud layers.

**IFR/VFR categories.** METARs map to four flight condition categories: (1) **LIFR**: ceiling below 500 AGL and/or visibility below 1 SM. (2) **IFR**: ceiling 500-999 AGL and/or visibility 1-3 SM. (3) **MVFR** (Marginal VFR): ceiling 1,000-3,000 AGL and/or visibility 3-5 SM. (4) **VFR**: ceiling above 3,000 AGL and visibility above 5 SM.

**SPECIs — the unscheduled urgent update.** METARs are issued every hour. A SPECI is an unscheduled METAR issued when conditions change rapidly: ceiling or visibility drops below select thresholds, a tornado is spotted, wind shear is reported, or precipitation begins or ends. If you receive a METAR from 35 minutes ago and the sequence hasn't updated, check whether conditions have changed enough to trigger a SPECI.

**The checkride trap:** Two classics. First: the DPE points to a 'SCT030' sky condition and asks 'Is that a ceiling?' No — scattered is not a ceiling. BKN or OVC is. Second: they ask you to determine if a flight is legal VFR given a METAR with 'OVC015.' Ceiling is 1,500 AGL. This is IFR in controlled airspace. The answer: no go without Special VFR — and night SVFR requires an instrument rating.
